question: How long should a simple phone number port take under FCC rules?
reference: FCC rules require simple ports to be processed in one business day. Ports between wireless providers may work within a few hours, while porting from wireline to wireless may take a few days.

question: Can my old phone company refuse to transfer my number to a new carrier because I still owe it money?
reference: No. Once you request service from a new company, your old company cannot refuse to port your number, even if you owe an outstanding balance or a termination fee.

question: I'm moving to a different part of the country. Can I always keep my landline number when I change providers?
reference: Not always. If you move to a new geographic area you may not be able to keep your number, and some rural wireline providers have waivers from the porting requirement; in that case contact your state public utilities commission.

question: If a phone company slams me, do I have to pay its charges?
reference: Under FCC rules you don't have to pay the slamming company for the first 30 days of its service. You should also ask your authorized company to switch you back to your previous plan and remove any switching charges.

question: What is cramming on a telephone bill?
reference: Cramming is the illegal act of placing unauthorized charges on a wireline, wireless or bundled-services telephone bill, often relying on confusing bills to trick consumers into paying for services they did not authorize or receive.

question: A charge on my phone bill is for something that isn't a telephone service and I think it's wrong. Where can I complain if the company won't fix it?
reference: First contact the billing company or service provider. If not satisfied, complaints about non-telephone services on a phone bill go to the Federal Trade Commission.

question: Why might my wireless bill be higher after I use my phone outside my plan's network area?
reference: Because of roaming charges: wireless providers typically charge higher per-minute rates for calls made or received outside the service area or network in your plan, and may add charges such as a daily access fee.

question: Are the 'access charges' on my phone bill a government tax?
reference: No. Access charges let local telephone companies bill customers for part of the cost of providing access to their local networks. They are not a government charge or tax; the FCC sets the maximum, and companies may charge less or nothing.

question: Does a telemarketer need my permission before making a prerecorded sales call to my cell phone?
reference: Yes. FCC rules require prior written consent, on paper or electronically (including website forms or a keypress), before a prerecorded telemarketing call to a home or wireless number; this does not apply to emergency calls about danger to life, safety or property.

question: Are robocalls that use an AI-generated or cloned voice legal?
reference: AI-generated voice calls are illegal unless the consumer has agreed to receive them or the caller is exempt.

question: A caller says I owe a government fee and must pay with gift cards. What should I do?
reference: Treat it as a scam: if a caller asks you to pay with gift cards it's a scam. Hang up, don't share personal or account information, and if they claim to be from an agency, call back using an official number from a statement or the agency's website.

question: Why do some scammers let my phone ring only once and then hang up?
reference: In the 'one ring' scam they want you to call back. The number may be international, so calling back can connect you outside the U.S. and charge a connection fee plus significant per-minute fees, which may appear on your bill as premium services.

question: I never make international calls. What can I ask my phone company to do to protect myself from one-ring scams?
reference: Ask your local or wireless phone company to block outgoing international calls on your line.

question: What is caller ID spoofing?
reference: Spoofing is when a caller deliberately falsifies the information sent to your caller ID display to disguise their identity, for example using 'neighbor spoofing' to look like a local number or spoofing a trusted company or agency.

question: Someone calls collect saying they are a relative in Mexico. How can I check it's really my family member?
reference: Ask the operator to have the person placing the collect call speak their own name so you might recognize the voice, instead of letting the operator say the name. You can also use caller ID to screen calls, and be careful because numbers can be spoofed.

question: How do hackers misuse voicemail boxes that still have the default password?
reference: They break into mailboxes with default or easy passwords, change the greeting to something like 'Yes, operator, I will accept the charges', and then place collect calls that automated systems accept, using the connection to make international calls at the owner's expense.

question: In an emergency, should I text 911 or call?
reference: Call if you can. Voice calls give 911 centers more information and are the most reliable and preferred method; text-to-911 is only available in certain locations.

question: Once a 911 call center requests text-to-911, how long do text messaging providers have to deliver it?
reference: Six months.

question: Do I have to pay or sign up to receive Wireless Emergency Alerts?
reference: No. WEA alerts are free and consumers do not need to sign up; they are delivered to WEA-capable devices if the wireless carrier participates.

question: Is an eSIM more secure than a removable SIM card?
reference: Yes. An eSIM cannot be stolen without stealing the phone, while removable SIM cards are sometimes stolen and used in port-out scams.

question: How can I stay safe when using public Wi-Fi hotspots?
reference: Watch for imposter hotspots, only exchange information with https websites, don't auto-connect to untrusted networks, consider a VPN if you use public Wi-Fi regularly, and use your cellphone data plan for sensitive information.

question: What minimum download speed does the FCC suggest for streaming 4K Ultra HD video?
reference: 25 Mbps.

question: What information do broadband consumer labels have to show?
reference: Broadband prices, introductory rate details, data allowances, broadband speeds, and links to more information such as available discounts or bundles, network management and privacy policies.

question: After the FCC sends my billing complaint to my provider, how long does the provider have to respond?
reference: The provider must respond in writing within 30 days of receiving the complaint, and must send the response to both you and the FCC.

question: Which federal agency, rather than the FCC, handles complaints about false advertising, scams and debt collection?
reference: The Federal Trade Commission.

question: My landlord only allows one internet provider into my apartment building. Does that break FCC rules?
reference: Not necessarily. FCC rules apply to service providers, not landlords, so a landlord may choose which providers it allows in, even just one. Service providers, however, may not enter agreements that grant them exclusive access to the building.

question: My cable company started charging me for a premium channel I never asked for. Is that allowed?
reference: Generally no. This is 'negative option billing'; cable operators are generally prohibited from charging for services or equipment the subscriber did not affirmatively request, and failing to refuse an offer is not an affirmative request.

question: What happens when I dial 711?
reference: Dialing 711 automatically connects you to a Telecommunications Relay Service communications assistant. It is free and works from any telephone in the United States, so voice and TTY users don't need to remember a ten-digit access number.

question: What is the difference between slamming and cramming?
reference: Slamming is illegally switching a consumer's wireline telephone company without permission, while cramming is illegally placing unauthorized charges on a telephone bill.

question: Can I still sign up for the Affordable Connectivity Program discount on my internet bill?
reference: No. The Affordable Connectivity Program and its monthly broadband discount ended on June 1, 2024; websites still advertising ACP enrollment may be misleading and can be reported to the FCC.
